topics.description: On-demand delivery of computing resources over a network, billed by consumption rather than bought outright.
On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service — the NIST definition.
Infrastructure as a Service: you rent virtual machines, storage and networks, and remain responsible for the OS upward.
topics.notes: IaaS/PaaS/SaaS is a named comparison and near-certain content.

topics.description: Platform as a Service: you deploy application code and the provider runs the OS, runtime and scaling beneath it.
Software as a Service: you consume a finished application and manage only your data and users.
Code runs in response to events with no server management and no charge when idle. Servers still exist; you simply do not manage them.
topics.notes: Removed as a named competency in the 2025 update, but still meaningful under Cloud Computing.

topics.description: Shared provider-owned infrastructure available to any customer.
Cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organisation, on-premises or hosted.
Public and private used together with workloads placed deliberately in each.
Using more than one public provider, often to avoid dependence on a single vendor.
Running multiple isolated virtual machines on one physical host, the technology cloud infrastructure is built on.
The layer creating and running VMs. Type 1 runs directly on hardware; type 2 runs atop a host OS.
A complete emulated computer with its own kernel and OS, isolated from its neighbours.
A VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own kernel; a container shares the host kernel and isolates only the process view. Containers start faster and cost less; VMs isolate more strongly.
topics.notes: A named comparison and very commonly tested.

topics.description: The provider secures the cloud; the customer secures what they put in it. The boundary moves with the service model.
topics.notes: Candidates routinely over-estimate what the provider covers, particularly for IaaS.

topics.description: A region is a geographic location; availability zones are isolated datacentres within it. Spreading across zones is the basic availability technique.
Provider-operated components — databases, queues, caches — trading control for reduced operational burden.
Object storage holds whole items addressed by key and scales enormously; block storage backs filesystems and VM disks; file storage presents a shared network filesystem.
topics.notes: Choosing the right one for a scenario is a likely question shape.

topics.description: Rehost (lift and shift), replatform, refactor, and replace — increasing effort for increasing cloud benefit.
Dependence on provider-specific services that makes moving away costly.
Web console, CLI, API and infrastructure-as-code are four ways to drive the same platform; only the last is reproducible.
The provider’s contractual commitment, typically an availability percentage with remedies if missed.
The proportion of time a service is usable, usually quoted in nines. 99.9% permits about 8.7 hours of downtime a year.
topics.notes: Translating nines into real downtime is a likely question.

topics.description: Designing so that no single component failure takes the service down, typically through redundancy and automatic failover.
Continuing to operate correctly despite a failure, with no interruption at all — a stronger property than high availability.
Duplicate components standing ready so that one failure is survivable.
Automatic transfer of work to a healthy component when one fails.
Scalability is the ability to grow to meet demand; elasticity is doing so automatically in both directions as demand changes.
topics.notes: A named comparison; the automatic-and-bidirectional part is what distinguishes elasticity.

topics.description: Making one machine bigger. Simple, but bounded by the largest available machine and usually needs a restart.
Adding more machines. Effectively unbounded, but requires the workload to be distributable and ideally stateless.
topics.notes: Scaling up versus scaling out is a named comparison.

topics.description: Adding and removing instances automatically against a metric or schedule.
Distributing requests across backends, with health checks so failed instances stop receiving traffic.
Keeping no client-specific state on the server so any instance can serve any request — the precondition for easy horizontal scaling.
Delay per operation versus volume per unit time. Optimising one can worsen the other.
Storing computed or fetched results closer to the consumer to cut latency and load, at the cost of possible staleness.
Geographically distributed caches serving static content from near the user.
Collecting quantitative signals continuously so degradation is visible before it becomes an outage.
The contractual promise, the internal target, and the measurement the target is judged on.
Locating the constraining resource — CPU, memory, disk, or network — before attempting to optimise.
Capital expenditure buys assets up front; operational expenditure pays as you consume. Cloud shifts spending from the first to the second.
topics.notes: A named comparison and a favourite of business-oriented questions.

topics.description: Billing strictly by consumption, with no charge for capacity you do not use.
Full price and full flexibility; discounted in exchange for commitment; cheapest but reclaimable at short notice and only safe for interruptible work.
topics.notes: Matching a pricing model to a workload is a likely scenario question.

topics.description: The full cost including staff, power, licensing and opportunity cost, not just the invoice.
Matching provisioned capacity to actual usage, the most common source of avoidable cloud spend.
Unattached disks, idle load balancers, and forgotten instances that continue billing after their purpose ends.
Providers typically charge for data leaving their network while inbound is free — a cost that surprises people repeatedly.
topics.notes: The asymmetry between ingress and egress pricing is worth knowing explicitly.

topics.description: Labelling resources with owner, environment and purpose so that spend can be attributed and cleaned up.
Thresholds that notify before a bill becomes a problem, rather than after it arrives.
Billing internal teams for their consumption, or merely reporting it to them to influence behaviour.
Tracking spend continuously and against forecast, since cloud costs change with usage rather than staying fixed.
Assuming components will fail and building so that failure is survivable rather than exceptional.
Spreading instances across availability zones so one datacentre failure does not end the service.
Provisioning through code rather than console clicks, so environments are reproducible and reviewable.
Replacing instances rather than modifying them, eliminating configuration drift.
Cloud-native accounts, roles and policies, applied with least privilege rather than shared credentials.
Storing credentials in a managed secret store rather than in code, images, or environment files.
Enabling encryption at rest and in transit as the standing configuration rather than an exception.
Provider snapshots and backup services still require a tested restore path and retention policy.
Recording who did what to which resource, which is the basis of both security investigation and change correlation.
Consistent metadata and written architecture so that ownership and intent survive staff changes.
A logically isolated network within the provider, in which you define your own address ranges and subnets.
Subdivisions of a VPC, usually placed one per availability zone.
A public subnet routes to an internet gateway; a private one does not and reaches out only via NAT.
Security groups are stateful and attach to instances; network ACLs are stateless and attach to subnets. Statefulness is the distinction that matters.
topics.notes: The stateful/stateless difference is the crux and is easy to get backwards.

topics.description: The first gives a subnet two-way internet reachability; the second lets private instances reach out without being reachable inbound.
Provider-assigned reachable addresses, optionally static so they survive instance replacement.
Managed authoritative DNS, often integrated with load balancers and health checks for failover.
Layer 4 balancers forward by address and port; layer 7 balancers can route on hostname or URL path.
Connecting networks privately, whether two cloud networks or a cloud network and an on-premises site.
VPN over the internet, or a dedicated private circuit, joining on-premises networks to the cloud.
